notes.front: What is threat modelling, in one sentence?
notes.back: Scoping a system's architecture and security boundaries, then analysing how elements interact across them to find risks.
notes.explanation: It is the primary mechanism for identifying which risks, controls and mitigations a cloud native system actually needs.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Modeling”
notes.example: Like drawing a building's floor plan before deciding where to put alarms and locks.

notes.front: What is a trust boundary, in one sentence?
notes.back: A logical line between zones of different criticality, where controls should be enforced.
notes.explanation: Threat modelling pays special attention to interactions that cross a trust boundary, since that is where controls matter most.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zones”
notes.example: Like the line between a shop's public floor and its staff-only stockroom.

notes.front: What are Kubernetes trust zones, in one sentence?
notes.back: Six logical groupings of cluster components by shared criticality, from a 2019 external threat model.
notes.explanation: Grouping components by trust zone, rather than by physical placement, is what makes the boundaries between them meaningful.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zones”
notes.example: Like sorting a company's rooms into public lobby, open-plan office, server room and vault.

notes.front: What is a data flow, in the trust-zone sense, in one sentence?
notes.back: A connection between two trust zones, described by its data, its protocol and how it is authenticated.
notes.explanation: Trust zones only matter once you know what flows between them, and whether that flow is verified.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zone Connections”
notes.example: Like a company org chart with arrows showing who reports to whom, and by what channel.

notes.front: What is a threat actor, in one sentence?
notes.back: A type of entity considered ahead of time when deciding which protections a system needs.
notes.explanation: Defining actors in advance lets a threat model reuse the same set of possible attackers across every finding.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”
notes.example: Like a heist film casting its suspects before the plot: insider, outsider, or someone in between.

notes.front: What is STRIDE, in one sentence?
notes.back: A mature model of six threat categories: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
notes.explanation: STRIDE gives threat modelling a checklist of threat types to consider for each part of a system.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”
notes.example: Like a pilot's pre-flight checklist, but each item is a way an attacker could win.

notes.front: What is an attack tree, in one sentence?
notes.back: A branching, hierarchical structure showing the different ways an attacker could reach a particular goal.
notes.explanation: Attack trees make the many small steps of an attack visible, so each branch can be mitigated on its own.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “attack tree”
notes.example: Like a choose-your-own-adventure book, but every page is a step towards compromising a system.

notes.front: What is persistence, as a Kubernetes threat, in one sentence?
notes.back: An attacker keeping a foothold in the cluster that survives Pod, container and node restarts.
notes.explanation: A one-off compromise is far less dangerous to an organisation than one the attacker can keep returning to.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Establish Persistence
notes.example: Like a burglar copying a house key instead of climbing back through the same broken window.

notes.front: What is denial of service (DoS), in one sentence?
notes.back: Preventing authorised access to resources, or delaying time-critical operations.
notes.explanation: In a cluster this can come from resource exhaustion inside a container, or from flooding control plane endpoints.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “denial of service (DoS)”
notes.example: Like jamming a shop's till queue so genuine customers can never reach the counter.

notes.front: What is malicious code execution, as a Kubernetes threat, in one sentence?
notes.back: An attacker running their own code inside a container, often via a vulnerable application or a poisoned image.
notes.explanation: This is frequently the very first foothold an attacker gets into a cluster.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Malicious Code Execution
notes.example: Like a smuggled note that, once opened, starts giving its own instructions.

notes.front: What is the compromised container scenario, in one sentence?
notes.back: A named attack-tree scenario starting from a vulnerable application in a container, often exploited through its mounted service account token.
notes.explanation: It models one of the most common real starting points for an attack: a bug in the application itself.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Scenario: Compromised application leads to foothold in container
notes.example: Like a shop's front door being left open because a cheap lock (the app) failed, not the vault behind it.

notes.front: What is the “attacker on the network” scenario, in one sentence?
notes.back: An attack-tree scenario for an internal attacker on the cluster's network who has no direct cluster access yet.
notes.explanation: It models an internal attacker who has reached the network but must still work their way into the cluster itself.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Scenario: Attacker on the Network
notes.example: Like a stranger who has slipped into an office building's corridor, but has no keycard for any door yet.

notes.front: What does “access to sensitive data” cover, as a Kubernetes threat, in one sentence?
notes.back: Reading data an attacker should not see, chiefly by exploiting misconfigured RBAC, but also via logs or eavesdropping.
notes.explanation: This attack tree centres on Secrets, since misreading them is the most direct route to sensitive data.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Access Sensitive Data
notes.example: Like reading confidential files left on an unlocked shared drive rather than breaking into a safe.

notes.front: What is privilege escalation, in one sentence?
notes.back: Gaining higher privileges than originally granted, such as breaking out of a container to the host, or abusing RBAC.
notes.explanation: It is often the goal that follows an initial foothold: turning limited access into much broader control.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Matrix for Containers”
notes.example: Like a visitor's day pass somehow letting them into the executive suite.

notes.front: What is MITRE ATT&CK for Containers, in one sentence?
notes.back: A matrix of attacker tactics (columns) and techniques (rows) that specifically target containers and orchestrators.
notes.explanation: It gives threat modelling a shared, detailed vocabulary for how real attackers actually operate against containers.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, "Threat Matrix for Containers"
notes.example: Like a criminology textbook's table of burglary methods, organised by stage of the crime.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · attack.mitre.org Containers matrix as of that date

notes.front: What is meant by fork bomb / cryptomining threats, in one sentence?
notes.back: Workloads that intentionally exhaust node resources, which requests and limits enforced via cgroups help prevent.
notes.explanation: This is denial of service turned inward: the attacker's own workload consumes the resources other workloads need.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Resource Requests and Limits”
notes.example: Like one tenant running every tap in a shared building until the water pressure drops for everyone.

notes.front: What is threat intelligence, in one sentence?
notes.back: Information about threats and threat actors, such as IP addresses, domains, hashes and tactics, used to help identify attacks.
notes.explanation: It supplies the indicators that runtime detection and monitoring tools compare live activity against.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Intelligence”
notes.example: Like a neighbourhood watch newsletter listing the makes of car recently used in break-ins.

notes.front: In STRIDE, what cloud native example illustrates “Spoofing”?
notes.back: Stealing a cluster admin's authentication credentials via a social engineering attack.
notes.explanation: STRIDE's six categories each need a concrete cloud native example to be useful in practice.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: In STRIDE, what cloud native example illustrates “Tampering”?
notes.back: Tampering with an API server config file or certificate, which could break API server restart or mutual TLS.
notes.explanation: STRIDE's six categories each need a concrete cloud native example to be useful in practice.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: In STRIDE, what cloud native example illustrates “Repudiation”?
notes.back: Disabled or misconfigured API auditing leaving no evidence that an attack happened.
notes.explanation: STRIDE's six categories each need a concrete cloud native example to be useful in practice.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: In STRIDE, what cloud native example illustrates “Information disclosure”?
notes.back: A compromised workload exfiltrating data to an external entity.
notes.explanation: STRIDE's six categories each need a concrete cloud native example to be useful in practice.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: In STRIDE, what cloud native example illustrates “Denial of Service”?
notes.back: A workload with no resource limits consuming all CPU and memory on a node, so the node is lost.
notes.explanation: STRIDE's six categories each need a concrete cloud native example to be useful in practice.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: In STRIDE, what cloud native example illustrates “Elevation of privilege”?
notes.back: A workload running with unrestricted privileges, or its security context being modified.
notes.explanation: STRIDE's six categories each need a concrete cloud native example to be useful in practice.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: What does the “Internet” trust zone contain?
notes.back: The externally facing, wider internet zone: kubectl and application clients.
notes.explanation: The 2019 threat model divides a cluster into exactly six trust zones by shared criticality.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zones”

notes.front: What does the “API Server” trust zone contain?
notes.back: The central coordinator, exposed only as much as needed for administrator access: kube-apiserver.
notes.explanation: The 2019 threat model divides a cluster into exactly six trust zones by shared criticality.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zones”

notes.front: What does the “Master Components” trust zone contain?
notes.back: Internal parts of the control plane that work via callbacks to the API server: kube-controller-manager, cloud-controller-manager.
notes.explanation: The 2019 threat model divides a cluster into exactly six trust zones by shared criticality.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zones”

notes.front: What does the “Master Data” trust zone contain?
notes.back: The data layer of the API server: etcd, tantamount to administrative access to the cluster if uncontrolled.
notes.explanation: The 2019 threat model divides a cluster into exactly six trust zones by shared criticality.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zones”

notes.front: What does the “Worker” trust zone contain?
notes.back: Everything needed to run and network containers: kubelet and kube-proxy.
notes.explanation: The 2019 threat model divides a cluster into exactly six trust zones by shared criticality.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zones”

notes.front: What does the “Container” trust zone contain?
notes.back: The actual Linux containers themselves, run by the container runtime.
notes.explanation: The 2019 threat model divides a cluster into exactly six trust zones by shared criticality.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zones”

notes.front: Is “Master Components” and “Master Data” still the current Kubernetes terminology?
notes.back: No: these are legacy names from the 2019 threat model; the current term is “control plane”.
notes.explanation: Current Kubernetes docs say "control plane" instead of "master".
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zones”; Kubernetes documentation, Glossary, "control plane"

notes.front: How is the data flow from the API Server to Master Data (etcd) authenticated?
notes.back: Over an encrypted, authenticated connection (TLS), verified: kube-apiserver retrieving and storing data from etcd.
notes.explanation: This is one of the best-protected flows: verified and encrypted, matching the sensitivity of etcd's contents.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zone Connections”

notes.front: The data flow from the API Server to the Worker zone, for log and status retrieval from kubelet, runs over {{c1::plain HTTP, unverified}}.
notes.explanation: 2019 threat model value; current docs describe HTTPS, with the kubelet's certificate unverified by default.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zone Connections”

notes.front: How is the Internet-to-API-Server data flow (kubectl administration) authenticated?
notes.back: Over an encrypted, authenticated connection (TLS), verified, and possibly two-way TLS, potentially via a bastion host.
notes.explanation: This is the main entry point administrators use, so it carries the strongest authentication of the internet-facing flows.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zone Connections”

notes.front: How does the kubelet schedule containers for execution, in trust-zone terms?
notes.back: Via interprocess communication, from the Worker zone to the Container zone, with no external authentication (not applicable).
notes.explanation: This flow stays entirely on the same node, which is why it has no network-level authentication of its own.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zone Connections”

notes.front: In the whitepaper's threat-actor vocabulary, who is the “Malicious insider”?
notes.back: An actor with malicious intent who has authorisation to perform actions within the modelled system.
notes.explanation: Other actors, such as uninformed outsiders, can be added; controls for them are usually a subset of those for these three.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: In the whitepaper's threat-actor vocabulary, who is the “Uninformed insider”?
notes.back: An actor with authorisation to perform actions within the system, who can be duped into causing harm.
notes.explanation: Other actors, such as uninformed outsiders, can be added; controls for them are usually a subset of those for these three.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: In the whitepaper's threat-actor vocabulary, who is the “Malicious outsider”?
notes.back: An actor with malicious intent, outside the system, attacking via the internet, supply chain or physical perimeter.
notes.explanation: Other actors, such as uninformed outsiders, can be added; controls for them are usually a subset of those for these three.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: In the 2019 Kubernetes threat model, who is the “Malicious Internal User” actor?
notes.back: A user, such as an administrator or developer, who misuses their privileged position, or whose credentials are stolen.
notes.explanation: The 2019 model lists six actors; the whitepaper lists three.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”

notes.front: In the 2019 Kubernetes threat model, who is the “Internal Attacker” actor?
notes.back: An attacker who has transited one or more trust boundaries, such as an attacker with container access.
notes.explanation: The 2019 model lists six actors; the whitepaper lists three.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”

notes.front: In the 2019 Kubernetes threat model, who is the “External Attacker” actor?
notes.back: An attacker who is external to the cluster and unauthenticated.
notes.explanation: The 2019 model lists six actors; the whitepaper lists three.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”

notes.front: In the 2019 Kubernetes threat model, who is the “Administrator” actor?
notes.back: An actual administrator of the system, tasked with operating and maintaining the cluster.
notes.explanation: The 2019 model lists six actors; the whitepaper lists three.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”

notes.front: In the 2019 Kubernetes threat model, who is the “Developer” actor?
notes.back: An application developer deploying an application to a cluster, directly or via another user.
notes.explanation: The 2019 model lists six actors; the whitepaper lists three.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”

notes.front: In the 2019 Kubernetes threat model, who is the “End User” actor?
notes.back: An external user of an application hosted by a cluster.
notes.explanation: The 2019 model lists six actors; the whitepaper lists three.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”

notes.front: Why must every action of a Malicious Internal User be logged, according to the 2019 threat model?
notes.back: Because they are often privileged with wide access, so strong non-repudiation of their actions is essential.
notes.explanation: Logging alone will not stop a malicious insider, but it ensures their actions can be traced afterwards.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”

notes.front: What are the two major branches of the Establish Persistence attack tree?
notes.back: Reading Secrets to exploit other vulnerable areas; and leveraging misconfigurations after container access to survive restarts.
notes.explanation: Both branches aim at the same goal, longevity, but start from different points: stolen Secrets versus existing container access.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Establish Persistence

notes.front: What are the two main approaches in the Denial of Service attack tree?
notes.back: From a container compromise, creating extra workloads to exhaust cluster resources; and flooding control plane network endpoints.
notes.explanation: The left branch abuses the API server from inside; the right branch attacks control plane endpoints directly over the network.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Denial Of Service

notes.front: What is the most likely non-privileged route for creating a denial of service from inside a container?
notes.back: Leveraging the service account token to launch additional containers via the API server.
notes.explanation: Without resource quotas in place, this can rapidly starve the cluster of resources.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Denial Of Service

notes.front: How can users with rights to create objects cause a denial of service, according to Kubernetes RBAC good practice?
notes.back: By creating sufficiently large or numerous objects to exhaust etcd, especially in multi-tenant clusters.
notes.explanation: Resource quotas that limit the count of objects a user can create are the recommended mitigation.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, RBAC good practices, “Object creation denial-of-service”

notes.front: What is the most likely initial foothold in the Malicious Code Execution attack tree?
notes.back: A compromised application giving access to the container, reachable via a NodePort or directly from the external network.
notes.explanation: This entry point recurs throughout the attack trees, since it is often the easiest way in for an attacker.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Malicious Code Execution

notes.front: How might an attacker distribute malicious code if they obtain an image pull secret?
notes.back: By poisoning the image repository the secret grants access to, and distributing malicious code from there.
notes.explanation: This turns a stolen credential into a supply-chain attack against everyone who later pulls from that repository.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Malicious Code Execution

notes.front: In the compromised container scenario, what is one of the most exploited attack paths once inside a container?
notes.back: A mounted and insecure service account token, giving the attacker its permissions on the API server.
notes.explanation: This is why service account tokens deserve special protection: they are frequently the very next step after a compromise.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Scenario: Compromised application leads to foothold in container

notes.front: What default gap does the “attacker on the network” scenario assume, allowing broad access from any Pod?
notes.back: No NetworkPolicy is configured in the kube-system namespace by default, so all Pods can reach it.
notes.explanation: This scenario's threats can mostly be mitigated with firewalls and appropriate Kubernetes configuration, such as NetworkPolicy for kube-system.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Scenario: Attacker on the Network

notes.front: Besides misconfigured RBAC, what other two approaches does the Access Sensitive Data attack tree cover?
notes.back: Viewing sensitive data stored in logs, and eavesdropping on network traffic.
notes.explanation: Sensitive data can leak through channels that have nothing to do with the API server's own access controls.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Access Sensitive Data

notes.front: What are two ways a user who can run arbitrary Pods in a namespace could escalate their privileges there?
notes.back: Mounting arbitrary Secrets meant for other workloads; using arbitrary ServiceAccounts to impersonate other workloads.
notes.explanation: The Kubernetes documentation lists four such routes, all stemming from unrestricted Pod creation in a namespace.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Authorization, “Escalation paths”

notes.front: What two other resources, besides Secrets and ServiceAccounts, can a Pod-creating attacker abuse to escalate privileges in a namespace?
notes.back: ConfigMaps and volumes meant for other workloads, to obtain or change information meant for them.
notes.explanation: Any resource another workload's Pod can mount is a potential escalation route if Pod creation is not restricted.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Authorization, “Escalation paths”

notes.front: In the MITRE ATT&CK for Containers matrix, what do the rows and columns represent?
notes.back: Rows are techniques; columns are tactics, the attacker's end goals at each stage.
notes.explanation: Reading the matrix this way shows both what an attacker is trying to achieve and how they might do it.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, "Threat Matrix for Containers"

notes.front: What are the ten tactics in the current MITRE ATT&CK Containers matrix?
notes.back: Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Stealth, Defense Impairment, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Impact.
notes.explanation: This is a complete set, current as of the date below.
notes.source: MITRE ATT&CK Containers matrix
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · attack.mitre.org Containers matrix as of that date

notes.front: What tactic name does the 2022 whitepaper use that the live ATT&CK Containers matrix no longer has a column for?
notes.back: “Defense Evasion”; the live matrix has no Defense Evasion column, it instead has Stealth and Defense Impairment.
notes.explanation: Tactic names are volatile: always check the live matrix rather than trust an older document's wording.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Matrix for Containers” (tier B); MITRE ATT&CK Containers matrix (tier C)
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0; live-matrix part C · facts only
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · comparing the 2022 whitepaper with the live matrix on that date

notes.front: What developer practice does the whitepaper recommend against the Initial Access tactic?
notes.back: Implement mutual authentication for externally facing services, and limit sharing host resources such as host filesystem mounts.
notes.explanation: Vulnerable public-facing applications are the usual first step the whitepaper describes.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Matrix for Containers”

notes.front: What Kubernetes mechanism most directly prevents a workload from exhausting a node's CPU and memory?
notes.back: Resource requests and limits, enforced through cgroups.
notes.explanation: Without them, a single workload, malicious or not, can consume all of a node's shared resources.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Resource Requests and Limits”

notes.front: What kinds of indicators does cloud native threat intelligence typically use?
notes.back: Network or host indicators such as IP addresses, domain names, URLs and file hashes.
notes.explanation: Behavioural indicators, such as an attacker's typical tactics, techniques and procedures, can also be used.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Intelligence”

notes.front: An attacker tricks a cluster admin into revealing their login credentials through a phishing email. Which STRIDE category does this fit?
notes.back: Spoofing
notes.choices:
A) Spoofing
B) Tampering
C) Repudiation
notes.choicesExplained: B: tampering means altering something, such as a config file, not stealing credentials. C: repudiation is about denying responsibility for an action already taken.
notes.explanation: Stealing credentials to impersonate a legitimate identity is the definition of spoofing in STRIDE.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: An attacker edits the API server's TLS certificate file, causing mutual TLS authentication to start failing. Which STRIDE category does this fit?
notes.back: Tampering
notes.choices:
A) Tampering
B) Information disclosure
C) Elevation of privilege
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing has been disclosed here, only altered. C: no privilege has been gained yet, only a configuration broken.
notes.explanation: Unauthorised modification of a config file or certificate is a textbook tampering threat.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: API auditing is disabled, so investigators find no record of who deleted a critical Deployment. Which STRIDE category does this fit?
notes.back: Repudiation
notes.choices:
A) Repudiation
B) Denial of Service
C) Spoofing
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing about availability was affected, only accountability. C: no identity was stolen; the actor's identity is simply untraceable.
notes.explanation: Without audit records, an attacker's actions cannot be attributed to them: the definition of a repudiation threat.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: A compromised workload sends customer records to an external server outside the cluster. Which STRIDE category does this fit?
notes.back: Information disclosure
notes.choices:
A) Information disclosure
B) Elevation of privilege
C) Denial of Service
notes.choicesExplained: B: no additional privilege was needed or gained here, only exfiltration. C: nothing about availability was affected.
notes.explanation: Data leaving the system to an unauthorised party is exactly what “information disclosure” in STRIDE describes.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: A workload with no resource limits consumes all CPU and memory on its node, and the node is lost. Which STRIDE category does this fit?
notes.back: Denial of Service
notes.choices:
A) Denial of Service
B) Tampering
C) Repudiation
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing was altered, only exhausted. C: this is about availability, not accountability.
notes.explanation: Exhausting a shared resource so legitimate access is prevented is the STRIDE denial-of-service category.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: A workload's security context is modified so its container runs with unrestricted privileges. Which STRIDE category does this fit?
notes.back: Elevation of privilege
notes.choices:
A) Elevation of privilege
B) Spoofing
C) Information disclosure
notes.choicesExplained: B: no identity was stolen, only privilege gained on an existing identity. C: nothing has been read or exfiltrated yet.
notes.explanation: Gaining privileges beyond what was originally granted is the STRIDE elevation-of-privilege category.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: An attacker who has gained access to a container wants to reach the API server directly. How many trust boundaries must they cross, from the Container zone, in the shortest documented path?
notes.back: None: a Pod can reach the API server directly, using its mounted service account token.
notes.choices:
A) None; a Pod reaches the API server directly with its service account token
B) At least two: Container to Worker, then Worker to API Server
C) Four or more, always
notes.choicesExplained: B: this describes a different, indirect path; the deck's own compromised-container cards teach the direct one. C: nothing in the sources requires four hops.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes' own docs say Pods "can do so securely by leveraging a service account"; the control plane's default network exposure to running containers is also documented in the attack trees.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Communication between Nodes and the Control Plane", "Node to Control Plane"; Kubernetes Attack Trees README, "Compromised container"

notes.front: A penetration tester impersonates the API server to a kubelet, exploiting a documented flow. Which data flow does this attack most directly abuse?
notes.back: API Server to Worker: today the kubelet's certificate is still not checked unless --kubelet-certificate-authority is set.
notes.choices:
A) API Server to Worker (kubelet certificate unverified by default)
B) API Server to Master Data (verified, over TLS)
C) Internet to API Server (verified, possibly two-way TLS)
notes.choicesExplained: B: this flow is verified, making impersonation far harder. C: this flow is also verified, and the strongest of the internet-facing connections.
notes.explanation: Connections terminate at the kubelet's HTTPS endpoint, but by default the API server does not verify the kubelet's serving certificate.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Communication between Nodes and the Control Plane", "API server to kubelet"
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: Which trust zone does etcd belong to, and why is uncontrolled access to it especially serious?
notes.back: Master Data: uncontrolled access is tantamount to root or administrative access to the whole cluster.
notes.choices:
A) Master Data
B) Worker
C) API Server
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Worker zone covers kubelet and kube-proxy, not the cluster's data store. C: the API Server zone is the coordinator, not the data layer it talks to.
notes.explanation: etcd holds the cluster's full state, so the 2019 threat model treats access to it as equivalent to full administrative access.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zones”

notes.front: Looking at the trust boundaries diagram, which numbered flow carries the user's request into the API server?
notes.back: Flow 1, Apply Deployment.
notes.choices:
A) Flow 1, Apply Deployment
B) Flow 7, Poll for New Pod
C) Flow 16, Poll for services / endpoints
notes.choicesExplained: B: flow 7 is the kubelet polling the API server for new Pods, not the user's own request. C: flow 16 is kube-proxy polling for Services and endpoints, an internal flow.
notes.explanation: The diagram is from 2019, pre-v1.24; flow 8, "Docker run", is out of date since dockershim was removed.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, "Kubernetes Architecture and Trust Boundaries"

image.alt: A Kubernetes architecture diagram with numbered data flows between components: 1 Apply Deployment (User to API Server) through 16 (two separate flows share this number), an unnumbered Read/Write flow to etcd, red dashed lines marking trust boundaries around single components or small groups, and green lines marking machine segregation.
image.credit: "Kubernetes Architecture and Trust Boundaries", Kubernetes Attack Trees (CNCF Financial Services User Group), https://github.com/cncf/financial-user-group/blob/main/projects/k8s-threat-model/AttackTrees/images/trustboundaries.png

notes.front: A cluster administrator is tricked by a phishing email into running a malicious script with their own privileges. Which whitepaper threat actor best describes them?
notes.back: Uninformed insider: authorised, but duped into causing harm.
notes.choices:
A) Uninformed insider
B) Malicious insider
C) Malicious outsider
notes.choicesExplained: B: a malicious insider acts with intent; this administrator did not intend harm. C: the administrator is inside the system, with legitimate authorisation, not an outsider.
notes.explanation: The distinguishing factor between the whitepaper's insider actors is intent, not authorisation: both have it, only one means harm.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: An unauthenticated party outside the organisation compromises a dependency in the software supply chain to attack the cluster. Which whitepaper actor is this?
notes.back: Malicious outsider: outside the system, without explicit authorisation, attacking via the supply chain.
notes.choices:
A) Malicious outsider
B) Malicious insider
C) Uninformed insider
notes.choicesExplained: B and C both require some form of authorisation within the system, which a supply-chain attacker from outside does not have.
notes.explanation: The whitepaper explicitly names the supply chain as one of the malicious outsider's possible attack routes.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: Using the 2019 threat model's vocabulary, an attacker has broken out of an application into its container, but holds no valid cluster credentials. Which actor are they?
notes.back: Internal Attacker: they have transited a trust boundary, but are not an authenticated cluster user.
notes.choices:
A) Internal Attacker
B) External Attacker
C) Malicious Internal User
notes.choicesExplained: B: an External Attacker has not yet crossed any trust boundary. C: a Malicious Internal User is a legitimate, credentialed user misusing their position, unlike this attacker.
notes.explanation: The 2019 model's Internal Attacker specifically describes someone who has crossed into the system without holding valid credentials themselves.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”

notes.front: A card describes an actor as “Developer”. Which source uses this term?
notes.back: The 2019 Kubernetes threat model; the whitepaper's actor vocabulary does not include a Developer category.
notes.choices:
A) The 2019 threat model
B) The whitepaper
C) Both name it identically
notes.choicesExplained: B: the whitepaper only names malicious insider, uninformed insider and malicious outsider. C: the two vocabularies do not overlap term for term.
notes.explanation: The two lists come from different documents and do not map one to one.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”

notes.front: In a Confused Deputy attack such as Cross-Site Request Forgery, a normal user is tricked into acting against their own cluster's interest. What role can this user play, according to the 2019 model?
notes.back: Both victim and potential direct attacker, even though a secondary attacker enticed the action.
notes.choices:
A) Both victim and potential direct attacker
B) Only a victim, never an attacker
C) Only an attacker, never a victim
notes.choicesExplained: B and C both miss the model's point: the same user can be recorded as the (unwitting) source of an action while also being its target.
notes.explanation: The 2019 model deliberately notes that an enticed user can appear as the attacker of record, even without malicious intent.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”

notes.front: An attacker who has compromised a container wants a foothold that survives a Pod restart. Which underlying Kubernetes weakness are they most likely relying on?
notes.back: A misconfiguration resilient to Pod restarts, node restarts and container restarts.
notes.choices:
A) A misconfiguration resilient to Pod, node and container restarts
B) A missing NetworkPolicy
C) An unpatched flaw in the container runtime
notes.choicesExplained: B: NetworkPolicy affects network reachability, not restart survival. C: an unpatched runtime flaw is one possible entry route, but persistence specifically targets what survives a restart.
notes.explanation: The persistence attack tree's second branch is specifically about misconfigurations that are resilient to Pod, container and node restarts.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Establish Persistence

notes.front: A multi-tenant cluster has no ResourceQuota configured. A tenant's compromised Pod starts launching hundreds of additional Pods via the API server. What single control would have limited this?
notes.back: A ResourceQuota limiting the number of objects a namespace can create.
notes.choices:
A) A ResourceQuota on object counts
B) A stricter Pod Security Standard
C) Enabling audit logging
notes.choicesExplained: B: Pod Security Standards restrict configuration such as privilege, not object counts. C: audit logging would record the attack, but would not have prevented it.
notes.explanation: The attack tree names exactly this route as the most likely denial-of-service path from inside a compromised, non-privileged container.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Denial Of Service

notes.front: A public-facing web application in a Pod has a remote code execution bug. What is the most direct consequence, per the Malicious Code Execution attack tree?
notes.back: The attacker gains access to the container, the most likely initial foothold modelled by this tree.
notes.choices:
A) Access to the container
B) Immediate root access to the node
C) Automatic persistence across restarts
notes.choicesExplained: B: reaching the node requires a further escalation step, not modelled as automatic. C: persistence is a separate attack tree, requiring its own additional steps.
notes.explanation: A vulnerable public-facing application is described as perhaps the most likely initial foothold into a Kubernetes environment.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Malicious Code Execution

notes.front: To validate mitigations against the compromised container scenario, what should a security team specifically test?
notes.back: Whether the mounted service account token's permissions are restricted enough to limit an attacker who reaches the container.
notes.choices:
A) The mounted service account token's permissions
B) The cluster's audit log retention period
C) The number of nodes in the cluster
notes.choicesExplained: B: log retention matters for investigation, not for limiting what a compromised token can do. C: cluster size has no bearing on this specific attack path.
notes.explanation: The scenario's most exploited path is a mounted, insecure service account token, so testing its permissions directly validates the mitigation.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Scenario: Compromised application leads to foothold in container

notes.front: A cluster has no firewall restrictions and the default kube-system NetworkPolicy gap. Which control would most directly reduce the “attacker on the network” scenario's threats?
notes.back: Firewalls together with appropriate NetworkPolicy configuration restricting access to kube-system.
notes.choices:
A) Firewalls and NetworkPolicy for kube-system
B) A stricter audit policy
C) Rotating Secrets more frequently
notes.choicesExplained: B: an audit policy records events; it does not stop network access in the first place. C: Secret rotation reduces the value of stolen credentials, but does not address network reachability.
notes.explanation: The scenario's own assumptions name exactly these two gaps: no firewalls, and no NetworkPolicy for kube-system.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Scenario: Attacker on the Network

notes.front: A security review finds that a service account has `list` access to Secrets across a namespace it does not need. Which attack tree threat does this most directly enable?
notes.back: Access to sensitive data, via misconfigured RBAC exposing Secrets.
notes.choices:
A) Access to sensitive data
B) Denial of service
C) Persistence
notes.choicesExplained: B: excess Secret access does not by itself exhaust resources. C: it may support persistence indirectly, but its primary and most direct threat is reading sensitive data.
notes.explanation: Misconfigured RBAC granting broader Secret access than needed is named as the major approach in this attack tree.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Access Sensitive Data

notes.front: A user can create Pods in a namespace, but has no direct RBAC access to Secrets. They create a Pod that mounts another workload's Secret. What have they achieved?
notes.back: Privilege escalation, by mounting an arbitrary Secret in that namespace to access confidential information.
notes.choices:
A) Privilege escalation via Secret mounting
B) Nothing; Pod creation does not touch Secrets
C) A denial-of-service condition
notes.choicesExplained: B: this is exactly one of the documented escalation paths from unrestricted Pod creation. C: no resource exhaustion is involved here.
notes.explanation: Pod creation rights alone can let a user reach Secrets they were never directly granted, one of the named escalation paths.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Authorization, “Escalation paths”

notes.front: A user creates a Pod that uses a more privileged ServiceAccount than their own RBAC role allows. What can they now do?
notes.back: Perform any Kubernetes API action that ServiceAccount is permitted to do, effectively impersonating a more privileged identity.
notes.choices:
A) Act with the more privileged ServiceAccount's permissions
B) Nothing changes; RBAC still applies to the user directly
C) Only read access is escalated, never write
notes.choicesExplained: B: once the Pod runs with that ServiceAccount, its requests carry that identity's permissions, not the user's own. C: the escalation is not limited to reads; it grants whatever that ServiceAccount can do.
notes.explanation: Using an arbitrary ServiceAccount in a namespace is a documented escalation path precisely because Pods act with their ServiceAccount's own permissions.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Authorization, “Escalation paths”

notes.front: A cluster administrator deploys a CRD that lets ordinary users change which Secrets or ServiceAccounts a workload uses. What should the administrator have considered?
notes.back: That this CRD may open a privilege escalation path, since it lets users make changes in areas escalation paths rely on.
notes.choices:
A) A possible privilege escalation path
B) Only a performance concern
C) No security impact, since CRDs are user-defined data only
notes.choicesExplained: B: performance is not the concern raised here. C: CRDs can carry real security consequences if they let users touch privileged fields.
notes.explanation: The documentation specifically cautions administrators to consider escalation consequences when deploying CRDs that touch these sensitive areas.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Authorization, “Escalation paths”

notes.front: An adversary deploys their own malicious image to a cluster so their code keeps running across reboots. Under which whitepaper heading does this fall?
notes.back: Execution & Persistence.
notes.choices:
A) Execution & Persistence
B) Initial Access
C) Discovery
notes.choicesExplained: B: Initial Access is the first foothold, not maintaining control afterwards. C: Discovery is about mapping the environment, not maintaining a presence in it.
notes.explanation: The current live ATT&CK matrix instead has separate Execution and Persistence tactics; this card follows the whitepaper's combined heading.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · whitepaper heading vs current ATT&CK matrix
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Matrix for Containers”

notes.front: An adversary makes many GET-style calls against the API gateway to enumerate what containers and permissions exist. Which ATT&CK for Containers tactic is this?
notes.back: Discovery.
notes.choices:
A) Discovery
B) Credential Access
C) Impact
notes.choicesExplained: B: Credential Access is about obtaining credentials, not mapping the environment. C: Impact covers the attacker's final objective, such as a denial-of-service action.
notes.explanation: Auditing get calls of an API gateway is the whitepaper's own recommended way to detect this discovery-phase activity.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Matrix for Containers”

notes.front: An adversary uses compromised containers to launch a denial of service attack that degrades a hosted service's availability. Which ATT&CK for Containers tactic is this?
notes.back: Impact.
notes.choices:
A) Impact
B) Lateral Movement
C) Privilege Escalation
notes.choicesExplained: B: Lateral Movement is about spreading within the environment, not the final damaging action. C: Privilege Escalation is about gaining higher access, a separate earlier stage.
notes.explanation: The whitepaper names denial-of-service attacks degrading availability as its example of the Impact tactic.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Matrix for Containers”

notes.front: A shared node hosts several tenants' Pods, none of which have CPU or memory limits set. One tenant's workload begins cryptomining. What is the effect on the other tenants?
notes.back: Resource starvation: the cryptomining workload can consume the node's shared CPU and memory, degrading everyone else.
notes.choices:
A) Resource starvation for other tenants on the node
B) No effect; Kubernetes isolates CPU by default
C) Only that tenant's own workloads are affected
notes.choicesExplained: B: without explicit limits, Kubernetes does not cap a container's resource use by default. C: shared node resources mean neighbours are affected too, not just the offending tenant.
notes.explanation: Resource requests and limits, enforced via cgroups, exist specifically to stop one workload from starving its neighbours.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Resource Requests and Limits”

notes.front: A security team notices a container repeatedly resolving a domain name known to be used for command-and-control by a particular attacker group. What kind of information let them notice this?
notes.back: Threat intelligence: an indicator (the domain name) associated with a known threat actor's behaviour.
notes.choices:
A) Threat intelligence indicators
B) Kubernetes auditing alone
C) Pod Security Standards
notes.choicesExplained: B: auditing records API server requests; recognising a malicious domain needs external threat intelligence to interpret. C: Pod Security Standards restrict configuration, not network behaviour.
notes.explanation: Threat intelligence supplies exactly this kind of indicator, letting defenders recognise known-bad network activity.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Intelligence”

notes.front: An attacker reads a Secret to obtain credentials for a different, more durable part of the cluster. Which branch of the Establish Persistence tree is this?
notes.back: The first branch: reading Secrets from within the cluster to exploit other vulnerable areas for a persistent foothold.
notes.choices:
A) The Secret-reading branch
B) The container-misconfiguration branch
C) Neither; this is a Denial of Service technique
notes.choicesExplained: B: that branch starts from existing container access and abuses misconfigurations, not Secret reads. C: nothing here affects availability.
notes.explanation: The attack tree explicitly separates the more obvious Secret-reading route from the misconfiguration-abuse route.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Establish Persistence

notes.front: An attacker without any cluster access floods the kube-apiserver's exposed port with requests. Which branch of the Denial of Service tree is this?
notes.back: The right branch: performing DoS attacks by flooding the network at control plane endpoints.
notes.choices:
A) The network-flooding right branch
B) The container-compromise left branch
C) Neither; this only fits the persistence tree
notes.choicesExplained: B: the left branch assumes the attacker already has container access, which is not the case here. C: this scenario has nothing to do with maintaining a foothold.
notes.explanation: The right branch specifically targets network endpoints, distinct from the left branch's container-compromise starting point.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Denial Of Service

notes.front: A team draws their cluster's architecture but never marks where trust changes across it. What step of threat modelling have they skipped?
notes.back: Identifying security boundaries, so the model shows where trust actually changes and where controls should sit.
notes.choices:
A) Identifying security boundaries
B) Listing every container image in use
C) Writing an incident response plan
notes.choicesExplained: B: an image inventory is useful, but it is not what threat modelling's boundary-identification step is about. C: incident response is a separate, later activity.
notes.explanation: Threat modelling starts by scoping architecture and boundaries; without boundaries, the model cannot say where controls matter most.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Modeling”

notes.front: A security team wants to show every distinct way an attacker could reach “run code inside a production container”, so each step can be mitigated separately. What technique fits?
notes.back: An attack tree, branching from that goal into the distinct ways it could be reached.
notes.choices:
A) An attack tree
B) A single STRIDE category
C) A vulnerability severity score
notes.choicesExplained: B: STRIDE categorises threat types, but does not branch out every path to one specific goal. C: a vulnerability severity score rates one known flaw; it does not map out attack paths.
notes.explanation: An attack tree is precisely a branching structure for the ways an attacker could reach one particular goal.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “attack tree”

notes.front: A team notices one node repeatedly runs out of memory and drops out of the cluster whenever a particular workload is scheduled there. What STRIDE category, and which mitigation, applies?
notes.back: Denial of Service; set resource requests and limits so the workload cannot exhaust the node.
notes.choices:
A) Denial of Service, fixed by resource requests and limits
B) Tampering, fixed by stronger RBAC
C) Spoofing, fixed by mutual TLS
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing has been altered without authorisation here, only exhausted. C: no identity has been stolen or impersonated in this scenario.
notes.explanation: A workload with no resource limits consuming all of a node's CPU and memory is the whitepaper's own Denial of Service example.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: An attacker inside a privileged container breaks out to gain root access on the underlying node. Which threat does this best illustrate?
notes.back: Privilege escalation, specifically by breaking out of a container to the host.
notes.choices:
A) Privilege escalation
B) Persistence
C) Access to sensitive data
notes.choicesExplained: B: the attacker may then pursue persistence, but the act described here is the escalation itself. C: nothing about reading sensitive data is described here.
notes.explanation: Breaking out of a containerized environment to the underlying host is the documentation's own example of privilege escalation.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Matrix for Containers”

notes.front: Several different attack trees in this model all include a “Gain Access to Container” sub-tree. Why is this fragment reused so heavily?
notes.back: It is often a key point of entry for a wide range of attacker goals and scenarios.
notes.choices:
A) It is a common key entry point reused across many attacker goals
B) It is required by Kubernetes RBAC syntax
C) It only applies to the Denial of Service tree
notes.choicesExplained: B: this is a modelling choice about attacker behaviour, not an RBAC requirement. C: the fragment appears across several trees, not just one.
notes.explanation: The Malicious Code Execution tree explicitly notes that this fragment is heavily reused across the models for this reason.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Malicious Code Execution

notes.front: A user creates a Pod that mounts a ConfigMap belonging to another workload in the namespace. What have they potentially gained access to?
notes.back: Information meant for the other workload, such as a database host name stored in that ConfigMap.
notes.choices:
A) Information meant for the other workload
B) The other workload's ServiceAccount token automatically
C) Nothing; ConfigMaps hold no sensitive data by design
notes.choicesExplained: B: mounting a ConfigMap does not by itself grant another workload's token; that is a separate escalation path. C: ConfigMaps often hold operationally sensitive data such as hostnames, even if not marked as Secrets.
notes.explanation: Mounting or using ConfigMaps meant for other workloads is one of the documented escalation paths from unrestricted Pod creation.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Authorization, “Escalation paths”

notes.front: How do the whitepaper's and the 2019 threat model's threat-actor vocabularies differ?
notes.back: The whitepaper names three: malicious insider, uninformed insider, malicious outsider. The 2019 model names six, including Administrator, Developer and End User.
notes.explanation: The two lists come from different documents and do not map one to one.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification” / Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”

notes.front: How do persistence and denial of service differ as attacker goals?
notes.back: Persistence aims to keep a foothold alive across restarts; denial of service aims to disrupt availability.
notes.explanation: The DoS tree itself notes that DoS is "perhaps not the most valuable to an attacker".
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Establish Persistence / Denial Of Service

notes.front: How does the Malicious Code Execution attack tree differ from the compromised container scenario?
notes.back: Malicious Code Execution is the general tree for running code in the cluster; the compromised container scenario is one named starting point.
notes.explanation: The scenario zooms into one likely entry route (a vulnerable application) that the broader tree also covers.
notes.source: Kubernetes Attack Trees, Malicious Code Execution / Scenario: Compromised application

notes.front: How does STRIDE differ from MITRE ATT&CK for Containers?
notes.back: STRIDE is a small set of general threat categories; ATT&CK is a detailed, container-specific matrix of real attacker tactics and techniques.
notes.explanation: STRIDE helps you brainstorm threat types quickly; ATT&CK gives a much more granular, container-specific catalogue to check against.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification” and “Threat Matrix for Containers”

notes.front: How does a trust boundary differ from a data flow?
notes.back: A trust boundary is the line between zones of different criticality; a data flow is the connection that actually crosses (or stays within) it.
notes.explanation: You cannot assess a boundary's risk without knowing which data flows actually cross it, and how they are authenticated.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Trust Zones” / “Trust Zone Connections”

notes.front: How does the 2019 model's Internal Attacker differ from its External Attacker?
notes.back: The Internal Attacker has crossed at least one trust boundary, such as gaining container access; the External Attacker has not, and is unauthenticated.
notes.explanation: This distinction matters because the two face very different sets of controls: what stops one may not stop the other.
notes.source: Kubernetes Threat Model (Trail of Bits, 2019), “Threat Actors”
